Costa Rica’s Chemicals Industry Faces Severe Credit Freeze Amid Crisis

San José – Costa Rica’s chemicals industry is facing its most severe financial crisis in decades as a sudden credit freeze grips the sector, leaving manufacturers unable to secure the funding required for day-to-day operations and new investment. The crisis, which began earlier this month, has already led to production stoppages, layoffs, and warnings of further disruption from industry leaders.

According to the Costa Rican Association of Chemical Producers, more than 60% of chemical firms in the country have reported difficulties accessing credit lines from both local and international lenders. “We are seeing small and medium-sized enterprises especially struggling to meet payroll or purchase raw materials,” said association president Luis Arrieta. “If this situation persists, we could see permanent closures in the coming weeks.”

The situation was triggered by a wave of defaults on existing loans following a sharp fall in demand for key chemical products, including fertilizers and industrial solvents. The National Bank of Costa Rica has reportedly tightened lending criteria, citing increased default risks and volatile market conditions. “We have to be cautious in this environment,” a bank spokesperson told reporters, declining to specify whether the bank would ease restrictions soon.

Major chemical manufacturers such as Quimica Tropical and CostaChem have announced temporary shutdowns at their main facilities. In a public statement, CostaChem’s management cited “acute liquidity constraints” and warned that the company may be forced to reduce its workforce by up to 30% if credit conditions do not improve.

Industry analysts warn the crisis could further erode Costa Rica’s position as a regional exporter of chemical products. “The longer the credit freeze continues, the deeper the damage to supply chains and the country’s export reputation,” said Carla Hidalgo, an independent chemicals market consultant. 

With no clear resolution in sight, stakeholders are urging immediate government intervention to stabilize the sector and restore confidence among lenders.
